sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light rain and high elevation snow today across southwest Idaho.
- Widespread rain and high elevation snow late Saturday into Sunday, with the highest precipitation amounts across southern Idaho. A slight chance of thunderstorms Saturday evening.
- Cooler with gusty winds Sunday, then dry and warmer Monday through Wednesday. Slight chance of precipitation late week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An upper low remains off the Washington coast early this morning. With ridging over the northern Plains, our area sits in southwest flow aloft. Embedded within the flow, a weak system will lift north across our area today. This will bring scattered rain and high mountain snow showers to southwest Idaho late this morning into the afternoon, while drier air to the west keeps southeast Oregon mostly dry. Weak instability across south- central Idaho will support a 10% chance of thunderstorms this afternoon in the Magic Valley. Showers will end by the evening with dry conditions overnight. Precipitation amounts will be light, with less than 0.10 inch expected in the lower valleys and 0.10 to 0.25 inch in the central Idaho mountains, and light snow accumulations above 7000 feet. Highs today will be near normal with valley highs in the mid to upper 50s. Winds will be light in most areas. Skies will partially clear tonight, allowing patchy fog to develop especially where precipitation falls today.

On Saturday, the low will elongate southward down the coast before moving inland Saturday night into Sunday. Additionally, a cold front will strengthen over central Oregon and move east across our area. The low will tap into subtropical moisture over the Desert Southwest, with southerly flow ahead of the low transporting the moisture north into our area. A few showers will arrive during the day on Saturday, but the bulk of the moisture will arrive Saturday night into Sunday. The chance of precipitation will rise Saturday evening to around 60-90% in most areas with showers increasing from the south, transitioning to steadier precipitation overnight. There will be enough instability for a slight (15-25%) chance of thunderstorms late Saturday afternoon and evening across southern Idaho, capable of producing heavier precipitation. Temperatures and winds Saturday will be similar to today.

Showers will taper off from west to east on Sunday as the low moves across the area. Snow levels will be 6500-8000 feet MSL through Saturday night, falling to 5500-6500 feet behind the cold front Sunday morning. Light precipitation amounts are expected across southeast Oregon. Higher totals are generally anticipated across southwest Idaho, with 0.25 to 0.50 inch of rain likely in the lower valleys. However, there is a 10-20% chance of an inch or more of rain across the Boise Metro. The highest totals are expected in the mountains east of Boise with 0.50 to 1 inch of precipitation (locally higher amounts possible), which translates to several inches of heavy, wet snow above 7000-8000 feet and light snow accumulations down to 6000 feet. Highs will be 5 to 10 degrees cooler on Sunday with gusty winds developing in the afternoon behind the cold front. Gusts will be strongest east of Boise through the Magic Valley and continue overnight, where gusts 30 to 45 mph will be possible.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An upper level ridge will build across the region early next week, returning dry conditions and warmer temperatures. However, the decreasing sun angle and developing weak inversion conditions will keep highs near to only slightly above normal. A weak low should disrupt the ridge on Thursday with potential for another trough on its heels on Friday. These systems will bring a 10-30% chance of showers to the area. Temperatures cool slightly at higher elevations while holding nearly steady at lower elevations. Winds will generally be light through the week.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: By Wed an upper level ridge will build over the area ahead of another possible system moving across on Thu. For now, Wed looks dry and warmer ahead of the next system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Unsettled weather returns late this weekend and early next week. Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during this time. High uncertainty remains for the foothills and plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: For late tonight thru Fri morning main concern is how widespread dense fog may become along portions of the I-25 Corridor from Denver north to the Wyoming border and points eastward. HRRR has been consistent in showing fog developing over ern Larimer and Weld county by midnight and then spreading it southward into nrn portions of the Denver area by 3 am or 4 am. This fog would then linger thru the mid morning hours on Fri before lifting. In addition, soundings show some potential for drizzle as well.

Meanwhile, for the rest of Fri, the flow aloft will be SW with only isold showers possible in the mtns and far nern plains in the aftn. As for highs, readings will be in the lower to mid 60's across the plains, however, lingering low clouds could keep temps in the 50's over the far nern plains.

For Sat, little change is expected as SW flow aloft remains over the area. There still appears to be a weak disturbance embedded in the flow which may bring a chc of showers to portions of the higher terrain with an isold shower threat across the plains. Temperatures will remain in the upper 50's to mid 60's over nern CO.

Looking ahead to Sun and Sun night, there continues to be some uncertainty as to how an upper level trough along the West Coast evolves. The ECMWF and GFS now have a disorganized elongated upper level trough moving into the nrn Rockies and Great Basin by Sun night. Ahead of this feature, there will be quite a bit of subtropical moisture affecting the higher terrain, especially by Sun night. As a result, should see an increasing chc of showers over the higher terrain with snow levels dropping below 10000 ft late Sun night. Across the plains, it looks dry and windy thru Sun aftn as sfc low pres intensifies from ern WY into ern CO. By Sun night, latest data shows varying precip chances across the plains. For now, have kept in a chc of showers as a band of mid level QG ascent moves across overnight.

On Mon, the ECMWF and GFS have two main areas of energy associated with the elongated upper level trough. One piece stays over the nrn Rockies while a 2nd piece of energy moves across srn CO/nrn NM. If this occurs best chc of decent precip would stay mainly to the north and south of the area. Meanwhile, both models shows a stg cold front moving across the plains with gusty north winds behind it.

For Mon night into Tue, the ECMWF and GFS keep the two pieces of energy separated as the one piece over the nrn Rockies moves SSE across Colorado while the other piece of energy moves from nern NM into central Oklahoma. In addition, the GFS intensifies the upper level low as it moves into Oklahoma by late Mon night. The ECMWF has very little additional precip Mon night into Tue as much drier air spreads across the area. Meanwhile, the GFS has a band of precip over the ern plains Mon night but also decreases the chc of precip over the area on Tue. Winds will remain gusty over the plains Mon night into early Tue as well.
By Wed an upper level ridge will build over the area ahead of another possible system moving across on Thu. For now, Wed looks dry and warmer ahead of the next system.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Midweek onwards, disorganized ridging is expected to build back into the area. Temperatures look generally close to remain fairly close to seasonal averages with lighter winds, though breezy conditions may remain in the typical wind prone areas.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Locally dense fog will persist over portions of the High Plains Friday morning. Another round of fog is possible Friday night into Saturday morning.
- Mild conditions are expected for Halloween (Saturday), though a few showers will be possible along and west of I-25.
- A complex but disorganized storm system will move into the area Sunday night, bringing cooler temperatures and a chance for rain and high elevation snow showers.
- Widespread blustery conditions are anticipated Monday into Tuesday along and east of the Laramie range.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: GOES satellite imagery this morning shows plentiful mid to upper level cloud cover streaming across the area with moist southwest flow continuing aloft. At the surface, a broad high pressure system over the northern Plains is supporting low-level south to southeast winds over the High Plains. This moisture flux has lead to the development of areas of dense fog along and east of I-25 once again. Fog is expected to clear out in the next few hours right around the immediate vicinity of Cheyenne as winds turn more westerly, but should hold on further north and east into the mid to late morning hours today. A Dense Fog Advisory has been issued for portions of the area, and may need to be expanded northward later this morning as fog spread further. Low clouds will be slow to break today in the Nebraska panhandle, keeping temperatures closer to seasonal averages. The most sunshine is expected to be found along the I-25 corridor to the WY/NE border, which should see temperatures warm into the low to mid 60s today.

Moisture return is expected again this evening into the overnight, leading to another chance for areas of fog across the High Plains, kicking off Halloween Saturday with spooky conditions. Trick-or- treat conditions look largely pleasant across the area this weekend. Temperatures will cool a few degrees Saturday compared to Friday due to increased cloud cover, but we should still comfortably reach the mid 50s to lower 60s for all areas. Model guidance is in good agreement showing a more notable vorticity maximum pushing into the area out of the southwest Saturday morning. This feature should support a few showers moving into Carbon county during the morning hours, and then spreading into Albany county, and possibly as far east as the I-25 corridor during the afternoon hours. Widespread rainfall is not anticipated, but expect to see occasional light shower activity, particularly in Carbon and Albany counties. Keeping an umbrella handy may not be a bad idea for trick-or-treaters along and west of I-25. Due to the high humidity, mild temperatures are expected once again Saturday night. Most areas will only drop to the mid 40s by 9PM before bottoming out in the upper 30s to lower 40s (a little chillier in Laramie as usual) Sunday morning. Sunday's highs will knock off a few more degrees with skies expected to become mostly cloudy by the afternoon. Southerly winds will be on the increase in advance of the next storm system which will approach the area Sunday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A complex storm system will bring a change in the weather for our area Sunday night into the early part of next week. This will be a fairly large and potent weather system, but two or even three upper distinct upper level low pressure systems moving across the west will make for a very messy setup. While a deep but somewhat narrow trough approaches from the west, another moisture-laden system will race into southern California along a potent sub-tropical jet stream. This system will get pulled into or around the primary trough as it moves through the area. Meanwhile, there is potential for another upper level low over the northern Rockies to drop down simultaneously, interfering further with each system. While moisture will once again be extremely abundant (NAEFS mean precipitable water values exceed the 99th percentile of climatology Sunday night!), this system will have the same issue as most others this fall: a lack of strong forcing to actually extract this moisture as precipitation.

Recent model guidance has trended largely towards the scenario where each of these upper level low pressure systems remain independent, with their forcing and lift interfering with one another. The overall evolution of the storm system has also trended more progressive and faster The net impact for our area is a decrease in the probability for widespread precipitation. While most areas can still expect some rain/snow showers with this event, the most likely scenario for QPF is fairly modest at this time. Greater than 75% of ensemble members have QPF under 0.25" for most areas inside a roughly Laramie to Glendo to Sidney triangle. There is still potential for between 0.25" and 0.75" liquid precipitation in Carbon county and along the Douglas to Chadron corridor, where forcing may be slightly more favorable. Still, about 25% of ensemble members keep the storm system too disorganized to deliver decent precipitation even to the Douglas to Chadron corridor, leaving most of the High Plains dry. Overall, confidence in expected QPF is highest for Carbon county at this time. There, extremely moist southwest flow can produce favorable orographic lift in the first phase of the storm system Sunday night into Monday morning, even if the second phase (the potential for wrap-around moisture) fails to materialize. Temperatures will be quite warm in advance of this system, meaning that snow levels will probably be as high as 9000 ft. Snow levels will gradually fall Sunday night and Monday, but there is a bit of uncertainty in seeing any precipitation at all after the colder airmass moves into the area. Probabilities for advisory criteria snowfall remain around 50/50 in the Snowy and Sierra Madre ranges, and about 25% in the northern Laramie range.

Regardless of the precipitation outcome, a cold front will sweep through the area Sunday night and cooler and windier conditions for most areas on Monday. Look for a rapid increase in northwest winds Monday morning behind the frontal boundary. There is fairly high confidence in widespread wind gusts of 40 to 55 mph along and east of the Laramie Range through much of the day Monday. Most of these areas have about a 20 to 30% chance for winds exceeding high wind criteria at this time. Temperatures will actually be several degrees below seasonal averages, only reaching the mid to upper 40s for most areas. Tuesday will bring temperatures closer to seasonal averages and continued northwest winds, but they should not be as strong as Monday.

Midweek onwards, disorganized ridging is expected to build back into the area. Temperatures look generally close to remain fairly close to seasonal averages with lighter winds, though breezy conditions may remain in the typical wind prone areas. There is potential for at least one if not two additional closed low systems later in the week towards next weekend, which may bring another chance for precipitation. However, confidence is extremely low at this lead time.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A cold front pushes through from northwest to southeast Sunday night into Monday, with snow levels dropping to around 8,000 feet by Monday morning and close to 7,000 ft by the evening as colder air pushes behind the front.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Precipitation chances return Friday PM with quick-hitting showers and storms for the lower elevations and flurries above 10,000 feet.
- Another round of 1 to 3 inches of rain for parts of southeast Utah and Southwest Colorado is possible Sunday into Monday.
- Flooding/flash flooding concerns increase Sunday into Monday, especially for areas that have saturated soils from last week's rain. A Flood Watch has been issued.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: ISOLATED TO SCATTERED SHOWERS FRIDAY AND SATURDAY:

A shortwave trough passes through the region Friday evening bringing a quick-hitting round of showers and storms to the region that will favor the higher terrain. Warm surface temperatures support rain being the primary precipitation type, with light snow possible above 10,000 feet. If thunderstorms develop, quick bursts of heavy rainfall could lead to isolated flooding issues, especially over areas still recovering from the last round of flooding.
WETTER AND UNSETTLED BY SUNDAY AND MONDAY:

A stronger surge of moisture an Atmospheric River (AR) arrives by Sunday. This AR will begin taking a southern track through Baja California, propagating through the Desert Southwest. There continues to be some uncertainty in the northern extent of the richer moisture, although confidence is high enough to introduce a Flood Watch for parts of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado that feature fatigued soils from recent rainfall and flooding. This is where there is the highest potential for 1 to 3 inches of rainfall Sunday into Monday. Please see the Hydrology section below for additional information on the potential for flooding and flash flooding with this system.

A cold front pushes through from northwest to southeast Sunday night into Monday, with snow levels dropping to around 8,000 feet by Monday morning and close to 7,000 ft by the evening as colder air pushes behind the front. Slippery stretches are likely over mountain passes. Keep an eye on the forecast if you plan to travel on Monday. Precipitation will taper off Monday evening, with cooler and drier conditions anticipated Tuesday and beyond.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: The system will push east of our area on Tuesday, leaving our area mild and dry with breezy north winds over the eastern plains, though less gusty than on Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Moisture will start moving into the San Juans today, with some scattered showers/storms over the far SE plains in the afternoon.
- Incoming system will bring heavy rain to the San Juans and San Luis Valley. Another round of flooding is expected for these areas Sunday-Monday.
- Accumulating snow is expected this weekend over the mountains, moreso Monday-Tuesday.
- A strong cold front will arrive on the Plains Monday, with winds in excess of 40 mph. Winds could prevail into Tuesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Have cancelled the dense fog advisory, as most locations have only light fog/no fog. Still could see some very spotty visibility near 1 mile along the Arkansas River through 9 am with some patchy ground fog.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Through the rest of the overnight hours and into this morning, fog will return to the eastern plains thanks to ample low-level moisture in the region.It should mostly remain east of Pueblo County, with reduced visibility around 1-3 miles with locally denser areas possible. Remember to exercise caution when travailing. Fog will clear around 10am.

This afternoon, a weak shortwave will pass just southeast of our area aloft, bringing up precipitation from the south. Scattered showers and thunderstorms will be possible this afternoon into early evening, mainly right along the KS border. While there will be a bit of instability out there, around 700-1000 J/kg of CAPE, no storms in our CWA are expected to be severe. Most of the precipitation will miss our area, staying to the east of us, though a few storms may drift over the CO border.
Temperatures will be in the 50s-60s across the area today, with breezy winds mainly out of the south and increasing cloud cover.
Moving into tonight,a trough will push into western Colorado, bringing the initial wave of precipitation into our western mountains ahead of our next impactful system.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The long-term forecast has come more into focus amongst the different model solutions, showing cooler and much more active weather into early next week.

Starting with the broader picture, two upper lows will be moving onshore, one from the Pacific Northwest and one on the southern California coast. The lows will phase with a broad upper trough, deepening and moving into our region by Sunday. Heavy rainfall will first spread over the San Juans, then to the rest of the Continental Divide and San Luis Valley prior to Monday. Some areas may see up to 2 inches or so of QPF during this timeframe, and with snow levels initially above 11 thousand feet, almost all of it should fall as rain. Flash flooding is going to be a major concern across the San Juans and portions of the San Luis Valley, especially considering how much moisture those areas have received recently. For the peaks of the mountains, again mainly above 11 kft, expect periods of moderate to heavy snowfall. Heaviest accumulations will be over the San Juans, with almost all of the recent model guidance showing well over a foot by the end of the event.

The upper low will pass overhead on Monday, dragging a deepening surface low over the plains and sending a cold front down behind it. This will spread precipitation across the plains while also bringing in some stronger winds out of the north. Meanwhile, cooler air will lower snow levels across the region, down below 9000 feet by early Monday morning before the system pushes east. Winds will be the main concern over the plains, with some models showing gusts up to 50 mph possible, along with widespread rain showers.

The system will push east of our area on Tuesday, leaving our area mild and dry with breezy north winds over the eastern plains, though less gusty than on Monday. Temperatures will remain somewhat cool towards the middle of next week, with highs dropping into the 50s, with breezy winds and decreasing cloud cover.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: In the wake of this system, mid level ridging will bring a cool and stable airmass into the area through mid-week, followed by another series of troughs beginning Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Tropical moisture will fuel showers and thunderstorms through this evening across much of Utah. Locally heavy rainfall may lead to flash flooding, particularly across southwest Utah.

- After a relative lull in precipitation on Saturday, an atmospheric river will interact with a strong cold front Sunday into Monday, resulting in widespread moderate to heavy precipitation across the region. This will increase the potential for flash flooding on Sunday across southern and eastern Utah.

- Accumulating mountain snow is expected Sunday night through early Monday as colder air spreads into the region. Local snowfall totals above 8000 feet may exceed 12" across areas favored in northwest flow.
- Cool, dry and stable conditions are expected Tuesday into Wednesday, before a more active pattern returns later next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A longwave trough resides along the Pacific Coast late this morning, anchored around an upper low spinning off the WA/OR coastline near 130W. A shortwave trough is noted ejecting through the lower Colorado River Valley, and is pulling an anomalously moist airmass into the Desert Southwest/southern Great Basin. Meanwhile an Atmospheric River (AR) is noted along the base of the longwave trough near 20N. This initial shortwave passage today, followed by the main upper trough late Saturday night through Sunday, will bring 2 rounds of heavy precipitation across southern and eastern Utah. The first round this afternoon/evening will be more convective in nature, while the second round late Saturday night into Sunday associated with the inland-penetrating AR will be predominantly stratiform. See the Hydrology section below for more details on the heavy rain and flood potential through Sunday.

As the initial shortwave ejects northward, ongoing convection across southwest Utah into northern AZ will lift into central and eventually northern Utah later this afternoon through this evening. In the wake of this feature, lingering moisture will maintain a chance of showers and isolated thunderstorms Saturday, however with the forecast area remaining between today's ejecting shortwave and the approaching longwave trough axis, large scale forcing will remain limited which will keep convective coverage isolated to perhaps scattered in nature.

As the upper low off the Pacific NW coastline begins its eastward progression late Saturday, the aforementioned AR will spread inland around the southern end of the Sierra, and into the southern Great Basin/Desert Southwest Saturday night, reaching southern Utah by early Sunday. The approaching upper low will translate through the Great Basin Sunday through Sunday night, with the combination of the two bringing widespread and potentially heavy precipitation across the forecast area Sunday through Sunday night. Colder air in the wake of the surface-700mb trough axis will spread into the area late Sunday through Sunday night, with snow levels falling from 9000+ ft Sunday afternoon to below 7000 ft by early Monday. This will result in accumulating high elevation snowfall across the forecast area Sunday night through Monday morning. Assuming the post-frontal environment evolves as currently forecast, a favorable orographic setup Sunday night into Monday morning looks likely across the upper Cottonwoods and other northern/central mountains favored in NW flow, where snow totals in excess of 12" are currently forecast.

In the wake of this system, mid level ridging will bring a cool and stable airmass into the area through mid-week, followed by another series of troughs beginning Thursday. Considerable uncertainty exists regarding how this pattern evolves beyond Wednesday, thus confidence is low regarding the probability, timing and coverage of precipitation later next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: An avalanche accident on the east side of Mt. Bross highlights that you can trigger a dangerous avalanche at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) of the Central and Southern Mountains. West, north, and east-facing slopes hold multiple layers of snow from several storms in October. Deeper, wind-drifted slopes may be the most enticing for early-season snow travel, but they're also the slopes most likely to release an avalanche one to two feet deep.

Clouds build from the southwest on Friday ahead of a small initial wave of moisture. Friday night, expect light rain below around 10,000 feet, and up to six or eight inches of snow in the favored portions of the San Juan Mountains by Saturday morning, with less precipitation to the north. Saturday, the moisture tap dries out, before a stronger storm rolls in early Sunday.

On Sunday, a deep east-bound low-pressure trough brings initially warm conditions, with snow levels around 11,000 feet. Sunday night into early Monday, a cold front intensifies snowfall and pushes snow levels down to around 8,000 feet. By the end of the day Monday, expect storm totals of 1 to 2 feet of snow in the San Juan Mountains with half that amount through the Central and Northern Mountains.
Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')
